messages.author: 9faf1380193a82a4
messages.subject: Implementing complicated models (defining custom functions?)
parts:
Hi

I am working on a problem where the model with which I'm trying perform inference is very complicated. In brief, the model describes the spatial variation of a measurable quantity over three (though possibly more) dimensions, and the model itself can be though of as being piecewise, with very many pieces. While I think Stan has the necessary functions and control structures to implement the model, the model file would be quite horrific to read. That is, of course, unless it's possible to define functions within the Stan language; from reading the manual, it doesn't seem like this is possible (am I wrong?).

What options are available to me if I want to use Stan? Can I define my own functions within the Stan language? Can I do so (sanely) by writing some kind of extension in C++?

Thanks in advance,

— Chris

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Implementing complicated models (defining custom functions?)
parts:
There's been a lot of discussion on this list recently about
what you need to do to interface a C++ function to Stan.

Short answer: If you can write a C++ function where parameters
are instantiated as stan::agrad::var and data as double/int
depending on type, then you can interface pretty easily.

This means all routines acting on parameters need to also be
defined for stan::agrad::var. You can use our stan::math and
stan::agrad and stan::prob libs, but it's usually a lot of work.

- Bob

messages.author: 2a7f346506a3e9ff
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Implementing complicated models (defining custom functions?)
parts:
Hi Chris,

The short answer is that no, you can't define custom functions easily in Stan.  If you're willing to hack the C++ (as Bob alluded to) you can add your own functions that way.  At a really high level, how to do this is described here: https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/wiki/Contributing-New-Functions-to-Stan  If you only wanted the function for yourself (i.e., not planning to submit it to the main repository), you can skip all the testing.

What you seemed mostly to be asking about was a way, in a Stan model file, to define a new function in the Stan modelling language.  This is not possible right now but is something we've talked about adding since Stan was first released.

That said, if you're willing to use the C preprocessor yourself, there is a way you can do this in your own.  Basically, use C preprocessor macros in a file, lets say called foo.stancp

#define FOOFUNC(a,sigma) a ~ normal(0,sigma)

model {
  FOOFUNC(x,sigma1);
  FOOFUNC(y,sigma1+sigma2);
...
}

and then, when you're building the model using CmdStan, call:

> cpp foo.stancp foo.stan
> stanc foo.stan 

Where the first call uses the C preprocessor on it's own.  If you're using RStan or PyStan this is still possible, but would be a little more complicated.

Cheers,
Marcus

parts:
On 1/23/14, 5:37 PM, Chris Rose wrote:
> Thanks, Bob, that's useful. And it would be great to see user-definable functions (and some sensible way to test and
> debug them) in Stan.

User-definable functions are on the short-term to-do list.

I'm imagining a syntax like this for functions:

simplex foo(vector x, real[,] y, int N) {
... local var defs ...
... statements ...
return result;
}

for a function that takes a vector, a 2D array of reals,
and an integer as input and returns a simplex.

And then for relational calls that could be used to
define submodels, something like:

void linear_regression(matrix x, vector beta, real<lower=0> sigma) {
sigma ~ cauchy(0,2.5);
beta ~ cauchy(0,2.5);
y ~ normal(x * beta, sigma);
}

So you'd still have access to the log probabilities where
appropriate.

We still have to work out the details.

- Bob

messages.author: 9faf1380193a82a4
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Implementing complicated models (defining custom functions?)
parts:
One comment on your proposed syntax for defining functions:

In general, I like the option to use named function arguments rather than argument order carrying this semantic information. This is something that I think R does well, particularly in the way it allows optional arguments to be defined with default values. I would not argue that argument names must be specified when calling functions, and that users who prefer using argument order to specify the meaning of the arguments could do so. I find named arguments make code more readable and lead to fewer bugs (e.g., no confusing standard deviation for precision when specifying a normal, for example). I note that named parameters is already used in Stan for specifying limits on values.

So, to adopt your example, what about the following:

// Define functions as you suggested:

void linear_regression(matrix x, vector beta, real<lower=0> sigma) { 
      sigma ~ cauchy(0,2.5); 
      beta ~ cauchy(0,2.5); 
      y ~ normal(x * beta, sigma); 
    }

// Optionally call functions using named arguments:
linear_regression(beta = 0, x = my_matrix, sigma = 0.5);

Best,

Chris
